newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU ministers to review U.S. trade sanctions.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers to review U.S. trade sanctions.

text.p: EU foreign ministers, divided in their support for President Bill Clinton's bombing of Iraq, on Sunday discuss how to react to Washington's plans to punish its foes in Cuba, Libya and Iran.

The ministers, holding informal-two day talks under Ireland's EU Presidency, are expected to discuss how to retaliate against planned U.S. trade sanctions on the three states which might affect European companies.
EU states are angry that two pieces of U.S. legislation will impose sanctions on non-U.S. companies operating with Cuba, Libya and Iran in contravention of free trade laws.
"We will be reviewing what retaliatory measures are open to us," said one senior EU official. "There are a number of things we could do that must be discussed."

European states are angered that their own companies risk becoming embroiled in American attempts to punish Iran and Libya for its alleged support for terrorism and Cuba for its failure to democratise under Communist strongman Fidel Castro.
The sanctions are enshrined in two pieces of U.S. legislation -- the D'Amato act, which targets Iran and Libya, and the Helms-Burton laws, which are aimed at Cuba.
The EU has threatened to take the Cuba law to the World Trade Organisation, set up to promote the freeing of world commerce and an end to protectionism.
The EU review follows intensive EU discussion on Saturday that failed to give Washington backing for its attacks on Iraq to punish Saddam Hussein for an incursion into Kurdish areas.
Instead EU ministers called on Iraq to withdraw from "safe havens" set up for Kurds after the 1991 Gulf War and said it backed the territorial integrity and sovereignty of all states in the region.
France had voiced reservations about Clinton's Iraqi raids, in stark contrast to the wholehearted support Washington received from Britain, its key European ally.
The EU said it wanted an oil-for-food deal with Iraq to go ahead as soon as United Nations Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali deemed that the situation on the ground merited.
The deal would allow Iraq to sell a limited amount of oil, despite international trade sanctions, to buy badly needed food and medicine.
Other items on what one EU official said was a "very packed agenda for informal talks" include the EU's own review of how to update its founding treaties to prepare the bloc for the next century.

Ireland is preparing a review of how each of the 15 member states believes the treaties underpinning the bloc's workings need updating which is supposed to be presented to heads of state at summit talks in December.
The eventual enlargement of the EU to absorb newborn former Soviet bloc states as well as a possible extension of qualified majority voting are among topics included in the review.
